claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has favorable plasticity and machinability but relatively low hardness and strength under room-temperature quasi-static testing.
The low hardness and strength of solid-solution CoCrFeNiTi are governed by high stacking-fault energy.
High stacking-fault energy in CoCrFeNiTi enables facile dislocation cross-slip.
Facile cross-slip promotes dynamic recovery during deformation of CoCrFeNiTi.
Dynamic recovery limits dislocation accumulation in CoCrFeNiTi.
Suppressing dislocation entanglement and deformation twinning limits strengthening and strain hardening.
Conventionally cast equimolar CoCrFeNiTi can be treated as a homogeneous single-phase solid solution with moderate grain size and no significant secondary precipitates.
Lowering the deformation temperature reduces dynamic-recovery rates in CoCrFeNiTi.
Increasing strain rate shortens the time available for dynamic recovery in CoCrFeNiTi.
Low temperatures or high strain rates may promote deformation twinning even in a high-stacking-fault-energy material.
High-strain-rate deformation of CoCrFeNiTi should produce a higher dislocation density and more dislocation alignment or entanglement than quasi-static deformation.
High-strain-rate deformation of CoCrFeNiTi may produce more deformation twins than quasi-static deformation.
High-strain-rate loading should increase the strength of CoCrFeNiTi relative to room-temperature quasi-static loading.
Lower-temperature or high-strain-rate loading should increase the hardness of CoCrFeNiTi relative to the baseline state.
Rapid dynamic recovery causes the low room-temperature quasi-static hardness and strength of CoCrFeNiTi.
The proposed mechanism is limited to single-phase, approximately equimolar CoCrFeNiTi and may change at low temperature or extreme strain rate.
Nanoscale ordering may also influence the mechanical response.
Failure of lower temperature or higher strain rate to produce concomitant increases in defect accumulation and mechanical strength would falsify the proposed dynamic-recovery mechanism.
